# Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

The central question is simple:

> What knowledge can the model carry so that the rest of the program no
> longer has to rediscover it?

The answer is to define meaningful values, establish their contracts at the
right boundaries, and compose operations that preserve or deliberately
transform that meaning. The following ten theses summarize the argument.

## 1. Type-driven design makes domain knowledge explicit

Type-driven design is a way of structuring thought: identify domain concepts,
admissible states, relationships, and operations, then represent them in the
values and contracts from which the program is composed. The mechanism in R
is runtime construction, validation, and dispatch, but the consequence is
larger than catching bad values. A named `DateRange` can retain the fact that
its endpoints are ordered; a raw pair of dates forces every consumer to infer
which is first, decide whether equality is allowed, and repeat the check.

S7 provides nominal classes, properties, validators, and generic dispatch for
carrying this knowledge. A useful model is therefore measured not by how many
classes it creates, but by how much rediscovery it removes. See
[Types and Meaning](03-types-and-meaning.qmd).

## 2. Nouns and verbs are co-designed

In S7's generic-function tradition, classes describe domain nouns and
generics describe domain verbs. Methods belong to generics rather than being
stored inside classes, so behavior is organized around operations that many
types may support. That mechanism changes the design process: a model is not
finished when its property graph looks plausible. Asking how values will be
`render()`ed, `combine()`d, `prepare()`d, or serialized often exposes a
distinction the nouns missed; a newly distinguished noun may in turn reveal a
clean dispatch axis or a law shared by several operations.

A good design therefore iterates between representative values and the
operations consumers need. Nouns without verbs become inert schemas; verbs
without meaningful nouns become branches over loose data. Co-design lets each
side correct the other. See
[Object Systems](01-object-systems.qmd).

## 3. Choose the substrate by semantics

S7 is useful for domain values with invariants and dispatchable behavior.
vctrs is useful for homogeneous vectors that must slice, recycle, and inhabit
data-frame columns. R6 objects and environments are useful for shared identity
and live resources. S3 remains effective for lightweight interoperability and
for designs driven by an existing external registry. The choice determines
which promises are natural: vector algebra, nominal contracts, or shared
identity.

Real systems therefore combine substrates instead of choosing a camp.
ellmer's R6 `Chat` owns an ongoing conversation, network activity, and an
accumulating lifecycle; its S7 `Turn`, `Content`, `Model`, and `Provider`
objects carry inspectable records and descriptions through that process. The
contrast is memorable because each system does the job its semantics fit.
S7 must earn its place through meaning, invariants, operations, or
composition, not merely through formality.

## 4. Separate editable values, read-only snapshots, and reference owners

An editable S7 value changes through replacement: an operation returns a
revised value while other bindings ordinarily retain the prior one. This
makes branching and history explicit—a draft can become two candidate drafts
without either candidate silently changing the other. A read-only snapshot is
also a value, but its public API intentionally offers no revision path because
it records a completed fact. A reference owner has shared identity, a live
resource, or an observable lifecycle, so aliases are expected to observe the
same change.

These are three lifecycle policies, not synonyms for mutable and immutable.
A draft document may be an editable value, its published form a snapshot, and
the editor coordinating both a reference owner. Copy-on-modify does not make
every S7 property read-only, and wrapping an environment, R6 object, or
external pointer does not turn the payload into a value. See
[Values and State](02-values-and-state.qmd).

## 5. Put each contract at the smallest boundary that can state it

Property definitions carry intrinsic shape, cardinality, membership, bounds,
and local presence policy. Class validators carry relationships among one
object's properties. Aggregate roots carry rules over contained objects and
references. Contextual operations carry checks that require datasets,
metadata, resources, or authority. The mechanism follows information
visibility: a scalar property can know that alpha lies in `[0, 1]`, but only a
style aggregate can know that every layer names an existing source, and only
an operation with runtime metadata can know that the source still exists.

Placing each rule once lets higher layers trust lower ones and keeps one
predicate from drifting across constructors, methods, and serializers.
Construction certifies only the invariants visible at that boundary and
preserved by supported transformations; it is a bounded certificate, not a
claim of omniscience.

## 6. Construction should retain knowledge

A useful boundary does more than reject bad input. Rejection says only “not
this”; retention lets later code rely on what was established. A `DateRange`
records ordered endpoints, explicit candidate values record tuning intent
that would otherwise be guessed from vector shape, and a prepared run can
record completion of data-dependent checks. The consequence is fewer repeated
questions: possession of the richer value answers them.

This is the dynamic-language form of parse, don't validate, with an important
qualification. Strict construction of known values can coexist with tolerant
parsing when uncertainty is represented explicitly as an unknown or partial
variant with diagnostics. Retaining uncertainty is still retaining knowledge;
silently collapsing it to a familiar value is not.

## 7. Alternatives, families, and failure protocols are separate designs

An S7 union states which alternatives a property accepts, and those
alternatives may include primitive or domain classes. Concrete classes
preserve variant identity. An abstract parent supplies shared schema or a
dispatch protocol, but does not seal the family. These mechanisms solve
different problems: acceptance, identity, shared behavior, and extension.
Coverage tests and loud fallbacks help detect unsupported cases; neither
proves exhaustiveness.

Failure adds a second axis that is easy to hide. A `Success`/`Failure` outcome
family represents what happened, but it does not decide what happens when
several outcomes are combined. One workflow may stop on the first failure,
another may accumulate all diagnostics, and an interactive boundary may turn
the same failure into an R condition. Modeling the failure shape and the
composition protocol separately prevents a sum type from smuggling in one
global control-flow policy.

## 8. One meaning may have several deliberate projections

An authoritative declaration can drive a native validator, schema,
documentation, UI description, or serializer. The mechanism is projection:
one owned semantic specification is interpreted into several artifacts. The
consequence is not infallibility but a smaller agreement problem. Instead of
maintaining five independent definitions, tests can check that each generator
faithfully projects the one source.

This makes generation from an owned semantic specification a legitimate
architecture. Blindly generating a class graph from incidental foreign
structure is different: it imports someone else's arrangement without first
deciding which distinctions have meaning in the R API.

## 9. Documents require explicit preservation and authority policies

A document is often a declarative program: a style, query, configuration, or
conversation transcript is data that another engine will interpret. The R
package is therefore closer to a compiler front-end than a bag of setters. Its
object graph should make meaningful constructions convenient, preserve the
distinctions required for a faithful projection, and delegate full conformance
when an external engine is the authority.

A parser, adapter, compiler, or serializer should consequently say what it
preserves, normalizes, loses, and compares. External authority may act as a
wire-format gate, a runtime metadata provider, or a test oracle. Typing depth
is chosen per node: semantic nodes with identity or operations deserve types,
extensible key spaces may remain validated bags, and embedded languages can
remain opaque until consumers need to inspect them. A schema is an important
compiler input and contract, not automatically the ideal native class graph.

## 10. General machinery must earn its keep; meaningful concepts need not

Every abstraction introduces a new place to look. It earns that indirection
when it absorbs a real axis of change: generic-to-method dispatch absorbs
behavioral variation across types, a semantic class prevents meanings with
the same primitive representation from being confused, and a wire-name map
contains serialization churn. A pass-through wrapper or speculative factory
with one use merely moves code without removing a decision.

The rule of three is therefore a useful restraint on generalized factories,
metamodels, and framework layers. It is not a requirement to leave an
important domain concept unnamed until it appears three times. Start from the
domain and intended consumers, sketch representative values and operations,
record the contracts encountered, and extract reusable machinery only from
real repetition. A large flat class or generated facade is not wrong merely
because it has many fields; the question is whether its shape is authoritative
and whether it makes its consumers simpler. Abstractions pay rent by deleting
rediscovery, branching, duplication, or coordinated change.

---

The remaining chapters develop these theses through mechanics, public package
examples, decision guides, and executable laws. The
[Doctrine](08-doctrine.qmd) compresses them for design reviews.
